Fiche_Unit1_WILLS_AND_LEGAL_MATTERS.title: Unit I — Wills and Legal Matters

options: A document by which a person disposes of their property after death
questions.explanation: A will (testament) is the legal instrument by which a testator directs the distribution of their estate after death.

options: Dying without a valid will — the estate devolves according to the statutory rules
questions.explanation: Intestacy is the situation of a person who dies without a valid will; the law then determines the heirs.

options: An advance decision/statement about medical treatment if one becomes unable to decide
questions.explanation: A living will (advance decision/statement) expresses wishes about medical care when the person can no longer decide.

questions.text: True or False: 'power of attorney' is the authority given to a person to act on another's behalf.
questions.explanation: True: a power of attorney (procuration) authorizes an attorney to act legally or financially for the donor.

questions.text: What is the difference between solicitor and barrister?
options: Solicitor: advises clients and prepares cases; barrister: pleads before the higher courts
questions.explanation: In England, solicitors advise and prepare; barristers specialise in advocacy before the courts (split legal profession).

options: Payment typically calculated hourly/weekly, often for manual work (vs salary, monthly)
questions.explanation: Wages are usually paid weekly/hourly to workers; a salary is a fixed annual sum paid monthly.

options: Dismissal because the job no longer exists (economic layoff, licenciement économique)
questions.explanation: Redundancy occurs when the employer abolishes the post — it triggers redundancy pay and specific procedures.

options: Termination of employment by the employer (licenciement)
questions.explanation: Dismissal is the employer's termination of the contract — fair or unfair; unfair dismissal can be challenged.

questions.text: True or False: 'sick pay' is the salary paid during illness-related absence.
questions.explanation: True: sick pay is the remuneration maintained during a justified sickness absence.

options: Leave granted to a mother around childbirth (congé de maternité)
questions.explanation: Maternity leave is the statutory absence granted to a mother before and after childbirth.

Fiche_Unit3_BANKING_FINANCIAL_PROBLEMS.title: Unit III — Banking and Financial Problems

options: The rapid outflow of capital from a country (fuite des capitaux)
questions.explanation: Capital flight is the massive movement of funds out of a country, usually due to economic or political instability.

questions.text: What is the difference between embezzlement and fraud?
options: Embezzlement: misappropriation of entrusted funds (détournement); fraud: deception for gain (escroquerie)
questions.explanation: Embezzlement is the theft of funds entrusted to one's care; fraud is the broader deception for unlawful gain.

options: Inability to pay one's debts as they fall due (insolvabilité)
questions.explanation: Insolvency is the state of a debtor unable to meet debts — it can lead to bankruptcy/liquidation.

questions.text: True or False: 'money laundering' is the process of disguising illegal funds as legitimate.
questions.explanation: True: money laundering (blanchiment) conceals the criminal origin of funds through a chain of transactions.

options: Trading securities using confidential inside information (délit d'initié)
questions.explanation: Insider dealing is trading on privileged non-public information — a criminal offence.

options: A company whose shares are listed on a stock exchange (société cotée)
questions.explanation: A quoted/listed company has its shares traded publicly on a stock exchange, unlike a private company.

options: To raise capital, increase prestige/visibility, and let shareholders trade their shares
questions.explanation: Going public raises capital from investors, enhances reputation, and provides liquidity to shareholders.

options: An owner of shares in a company (actionnaire)
questions.explanation: A shareholder holds shares (actions) representing part-ownership of the company.

questions.text: True or False: 'share' means a unit of ownership in a company.
questions.explanation: True: a share (action) is a unit of capital conferring ownership rights and dividends.

questions.text: What is a 'quotation' on the stock market?
options: The listing of a company's shares on the exchange (cotation)
questions.explanation: A quotation is the official listing/price of a share on a stock exchange.

Fiche_Unit5_TERRORISM_INTERNATIONAL_LAW.title: Unit V — Terrorism and International Law

options: The surrender of an accused person by one state to another for trial or punishment
questions.explanation: Extradition is the formal transfer of a suspect or convict between states under treaty or reciprocity.

questions.text: What did the 1972 UN debate on terrorism focus on?
options: The causes of terrorism and the right of self-determination of peoples
questions.explanation: The 1972 UN debate addressed both the condemnation of terrorism and its root causes, including struggles for self-determination.

options: The institution and conduct of criminal proceedings against a person (poursuites judiciaires)
questions.explanation: Prosecution is the legal process of charging and trying an accused person by the state.

questions.text: True or False: states condemn terrorism but disagree on its definition.
questions.explanation: True: while all condemn terrorism, states disagree on defining it — particularly regarding liberation movements.

options: The right of peoples to freely determine their political status and development
questions.explanation: Self-determination is the right of peoples to choose their sovereignty and political system — invoked in the terrorism debate.

options: Government by the people, directly or through elected representatives
questions.explanation: Democracy: power exercised by the people — direct (citizens decide) or representative (through elected officials).

options: A system where the head of state is a hereditary sovereign (king/queen), constitutional or absolute
questions.explanation: In a monarchy the head of state is a monarch — constitutional (limited powers) or absolute (full powers).

options: A regime where power is concentrated in one person or party without democratic control
questions.explanation: A dictatorship concentrates power in an autocrat/junta, suppressing opposition and freedoms.

questions.text: True or False: a republic has an elected head of state, not a hereditary monarch.
questions.explanation: True: in a republic the head of state is elected or appointed for a term — not hereditary.

questions.text: What is communism as a political system?
options: A system aiming at collective ownership of the means of production and a classless society
questions.explanation: Communism advocates collective ownership and the abolition of classes — historically through a single-party state.

questions.text: What is the difference between cash and deposits?
options: Cash = physical money (coins/notes); deposits = money held in bank accounts
questions.explanation: Currency/cash is tangible money; deposits are bank money (scriptural) held in accounts.

questions.text: What are the main types of income?
questions.explanation: Income includes salary (monthly), wages (hourly/weekly), commission (sales %), pension (retirement), fees (professional).
Outgoings are regular expenses (rent, bills) — the counterpart of income in a budget.

questions.text: True or False: a 'budget' balances expected income and expenditure.
questions.explanation: True: a budget plans the allocation of income against outgoings/expenses.

options: Payment proportional to sales or business generated
questions.explanation: Commission is income earned as a percentage of sales — typical of commercial agents.

Fiche_Unit8_THEORY_OF_INTERNATIONAL_RELA.title: Unit VIII — Theory of International Relations

questions.text: What event founded the modern state system?
options: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) — sovereignty and balance of power
questions.explanation: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) established state sovereignty and the balance of power — the Westphalian system.

options: The supreme authority of a state over its territory and independence from external powers
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the state's exclusive authority within its borders and its independence in international relations.

questions.text: What are the systemic tools of IR?
options: Diplomacy, sanctions, war, and 'naming and shaming'
questions.explanation: States use diplomacy, economic sanctions, armed conflict, and public denunciation (naming & shaming) to influence others.

questions.text: True or False: international relations only concern states.
questions.explanation: False: IR also involve international organisations, NGOs and transnational forces.

options: Coercive measures (economic, diplomatic) to compel a state to change its behaviour
questions.explanation: Sanctions pressure a state — embargoes, asset freezes, diplomatic isolation — short of war.

options: An organisation created by states through a constituent treaty
questions.explanation: An IGO is founded by states via a treaty/charter — it has its own organs and legal personality.

questions.text: When was the UN created and by which document?
options: 1945, by the Charter of San Francisco
questions.explanation: The United Nations was founded in 1945 by the Charter of San Francisco.

questions.text: What distinguishes an IGO from a mere group of states or treaty?
options: An IGO has permanent organs and its own legal personality, unlike a treaty or a loose group
questions.explanation: Unlike a treaty or an informal group, an IGO has standing organs and international legal personality.

questions.text: True or False: IO membership can be full, associate, or observer.
questions.explanation: True: states may be full members, associate members, or observers — with different rights.

questions.text: What is the 'constituent instrument' of an IO?
options: The treaty that creates it and sets its organs and powers (charter, statute)
questions.explanation: The constituent instrument (charter/statute) is the founding treaty defining the IO's structure and competences.

options: The strategy a state follows in its relations with other states
questions.explanation: Foreign policy is a state's set of objectives and actions toward the external world — diplomacy, alliances, trade.

questions.text: What is a 'doctrine' in foreign policy?
options: A stated set of principles guiding a state's external action (e.g., Monroe, Truman doctrines)
questions.explanation: A foreign policy doctrine is an official statement of principles orienting a state's diplomacy.

questions.text: Who conducts foreign policy in most states?
options: The head of state/government and the foreign minister — with exceptions (France: President; Finland; USA: President)
questions.explanation: Foreign policy is mainly conducted by the executive (President/PM + foreign minister) — in France it is a presidential domaine réservé.

questions.text: True or False: in France foreign policy is primarily a presidential domain.
questions.explanation: True: the French President holds a « domaine réservé » over foreign policy and defence.

questions.text: What does the Belarus/China example illustrate?
options: Different foreign policy postures and international responses to them (isolation, sanctions, influence)
questions.explanation: Belarus (isolation/sanctions) and China (assertive diplomacy) illustrate how foreign policy choices shape international standing.

questions.text: What does the 1949 Geneva Conventions protect?
options: Victims of war — wounded soldiers, prisoners, civilians — including the prohibition of torture
questions.explanation: The Geneva Conventions (1949) establish humanitarian rules of war: protection of combatants, POWs and civilians; torture is prohibited.

options: A person imprisoned for their beliefs/opinions (Amnesty International's term)
questions.explanation: A prisoner of conscience is detained solely for their beliefs, religion or opinions — Amnesty campaigns for their release.

options: Independent tribunal, presumption of innocence, defence rights, public hearing, reasonable time
questions.explanation: Fair trial guarantees include an impartial court, presumption of innocence, legal assistance, and a public hearing.

questions.text: True or False: human rights include both individual and collective rights.
questions.explanation: True: human rights cover individual rights (life, expression) and collective rights (development, self-determination).

options: Severe pain or suffering intentionally inflicted by or with the consent of a public official — absolutely prohibited
questions.explanation: Torture is intentional severe suffering inflicted for purposes like extracting confessions — prohibited without exception.

Fiche_Unit12_13_ECONOMICS_CV_APPLICATION.title: Units XII–XIII — Economics, CV and Application Letter

options: The economic sequence: needs → production → distribution → consumption → satisfaction
questions.explanation: The want-satisfaction chain describes how production and distribution meet human needs through consumption.

questions.text: What is the 'law of diminishing returns'?
options: Beyond a point, adding a factor of production yields progressively smaller increases in output
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns: adding units of one input (land fixed) eventually produces smaller marginal gains.

options: Personal details, education, work experience, skills, references
questions.explanation: A CV summarises identity, education/qualifications, work experience, skills and referees.

questions.text: True or False: a covering letter accompanies the CV to explain one's motivation.
questions.explanation: True: the application/covering letter introduces the candidate and their motivation for the post.

options: The quantities buyers want (demand) and sellers offer (supply), determining price
questions.explanation: Demand (demande) and supply (offre) interact to set market prices.

options: Words similar in English and French but with different meanings (actual ≠ actuel)
questions.explanation: Faux amis are misleading cognates: 'actual' = réel (not actuel), 'actuel' = current.
Deception = tromperie (fraud); French 'déception' = disappointment — a classic false friend.

options: A substance preserving food (conservateur) — 'préservatif' means condom in French
questions.explanation: Preservative = conservateur alimentaire; 'préservatif' = condom — a notorious faux ami.

questions.text: True or False: English legal vocabulary largely derives from Norman French after 1066.
questions.explanation: True: after the Norman conquest (1066), French became the language of law — hence attorney, court, plaintiff.

options: The mixing of English words into French (or the reverse)
questions.explanation: Franglais is the import of English vocabulary/expressions into French usage.
